wstep: This card follows the UGA Fresh Tarragon Vinegar: fresh tarragon steeped in commercially produced vinegar and kept in the refrigerator.

akapity: For each pint jar of vinegar: 3 sprigs (3 inches long) of fresh tarragon, or 1 cup of fresh tarragon leaves and stems.

UGA allows distilled white or white wine vinegar; this card uses distilled white vinegar, which UGA calls the best choice for delicately flavored herbs, because wine vinegars contain some protein that can support bacterial growth.
Use only commercially produced vinegar: wine and rice vinegars contain some protein that is an excellent medium for bacterial growth.
Vinegar with less than 5% acidity should never be used in home food preservation.

Do not replace it with a stronger vinegar and do not dilute a stronger vinegar with water yourself; Penn State Extension advises staying within 5–7% acidity for home food preservation and diluting vinegar only when a tested recipe says so.
Do not add more flavoring than this card gives: too much plant material can destroy the acid and ruin the preservative quality of the vinegar.
A US pint holds about 473 ml and a quart about 946 ml.
Wash glass jars or bottles in warm, soapy water, then sterilize them by immersing them completely in boiling water for 10 minutes; fill them with vinegar while they are still warm.
Close them with non-corrodible metal or plastic screw caps, or with new, pre-sterilized corks.
Wash the tarragon gently but thoroughly and pat it dry with a clean paper towel.
Lightly crush it before placing it in the jar.
Heat the vinegar to just below the boiling point, to at least 190–195 °F (88–91 °C).
Pour it over the flavoring in the jar, leaving 1/4 inch of headspace, wipe the rims with a clean, damp cloth, close the jars tightly and let them cool undisturbed.
Let the jar stand in a cool, dark place for 3 to 4 weeks.
Strain the vinegar through damp cheesecloth or a coffee filter, one or more times, until it shows no cloudiness, and discard the solids.
Pour the strained vinegar into clean, sterilized jars and cap them tightly.
Label each bottle with the base vinegar, the flavoring and the date.
Keep the vinegar in the refrigerator: some harmful bacteria may survive and even multiply slowly in some vinegars.
For best quality, use it within 4–6 months, as OSU Extension advises for refrigerated flavored vinegars.
Date the bottle when you open it.
Bottles kept as decorations on sunny window sills or shelves for more than a few weeks should be treated as decorations and not used in food.
If the vinegar shows mold or signs of fermentation such as bubbling, cloudiness or sliminess, throw it away without tasting it.
Do not use flavored herb vinegar for making pickles unless it has a 5% acidity level.
